survivors.title: Why Did Clorox Pay a $14 Million Fine? What Its Own Scientists Wrote in 2019 (2026)
survivors.villain: The Clorox Company. CPSC charged it with knowingly failing to report a hazard it was legally required to report immediately. Its own microbiologists wrote the problem down in early 2019. Consumers did not hear about it until October 2022.
survivors.receipt: On 2026-01-27 the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission announced that The Clorox Company agreed to pay a $14.15 million civil penalty to resolve CPSC's charge that it knowingly failed to immediately report, as federal law requires, that its Pine-Sol Scented Multi-Surface Cleaning Products contained a defect that could create a substantial product hazard or created an unreasonable risk of serious injury or death to consumers. CPSC states that in early 2019 Clorox microbiologists issued a written report documenting bacterial contamination in storage tanks and in finished product, which they described as "possibly a Pseudomonad." Clorox then received reports of cloudy product from certain retail stores, and a report from a distributor that cloudy product had been distributed in multiple locations. CPSC says that while Clorox took steps to mitigate the potential for bacterial contamination, it did not immediately report to the Commission as required. The recall did not come until 2022-10-25, when CPSC and Clorox jointly announced a recall of more than 37 million bottles of Pine-Sol Scented Multi-Surface Cleaner in Lemon Fresh, Sparkling Wave and Lavender Clean, along with CloroxPro Pine-Sol All-Purpose Cleaners and Clorox Professional Pine-Sol Lemon Fresh Cleaners, for possible contamination with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The recalled product was manufactured between January 2021 and September 2022 at Clorox's Forest Park, Georgia plant. CPSC said people with weakened immune systems or external medical devices face a risk of serious infection requiring medical treatment. Beyond the money, the settlement requires Clorox to maintain and enhance internal compliance controls under the Consumer Product Safety Act and to file annual compliance reports. Roughly three and a half years passed between what Clorox's own scientists wrote down and what shoppers were told. Attribute all of it as CPSC's charges and allegations, not as adjudicated fact. Primary source: https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/2026/Clorox-Agrees-to-Pay-14-15-Million-Civil-Penalty-for-Failure-to-Immediately-Report-Bacterial-Hazard-with-Pine-Sol-Scented-Multi-Surface-Cleaning-Products

survivors.villain: Cal-Maine Foods, the largest egg producer in America, along with Hickman's Egg Ranch and Versova. survivors.title: Is Roundup Safe to Use Around Your House? (2026)
survivors.villain: Bayer, which owns Monsanto. survivors.receipt:
On June 25, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 in Monsanto Co. v. Durnell that federal pesticide law preempts state failure-to-warn claims, so a company cannot be sued for leaving a cancer warning off a weed killer label the EPA approved. Justice Kavanaugh wrote the opinion, Justice Jackson dissented joined by Justice Gorsuch, and a $1.25 million verdict against Monsanto was reversed.

That win did not arrive by accident. Bayer, which owns Monsanto, spent two legislative sessions backing state bills declaring that a federally approved pesticide label satisfies any duty under state law to warn customers, which takes the failure-to-warn claim off the table before anyone can file it. North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong signed the nation's first such shield law, HB 1318, on April 23, 2025. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp signed the second weeks later, effective January 1, 2026, and it is now in force. Kentucky became the third in spring 2026. Bayer backed similar bills in roughly 14 states across the 2025-26 sessions.

The scale of what was being closed off: as of May 2025, more than 67,000 of a total of 181,000 Roundup claims remained outstanding, and Bayer had set aside about $16 billion to settle cases. In March 2025 a Cobb County, Georgia jury awarded John Barnes nearly $2.1 billion, $2 billion of it punitive, after he alleged Roundup caused his non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Bayer appealed and the parties settled on confidential terms in November 2025. Bayer disputes the cancer claims and says it has prevailed in 17 of the last 25 trials.

survivors.title: Is Redken Shampoo Safe? What L'Oreal Asked New York State For (2026)
survivors.villain: L'Oreal USA. New York capped 1,4-dioxane in personal care at 1 ppm. Instead of meeting it, L'Oreal USA applied to the state for waivers on 69 salon products and got them, listing Redken All Soft Shampoo at 4.5 ppm, Redken Color Extend Graydiant at 3.67 ppm, Kerastase Densifique Women Bain at 4.6 ppm, and L'Oreal Professionnel Serie Expert Volumetry at 7.23 ppm. That is seven times the legal limit, in writing, on a government form, signed by the company.
survivors.receipt:
New York's 1,4-dioxane law (Environmental Conservation Law Articles 35 and 37) and 6 NYCRR Subpart 352-1 capped household cleansing and personal care products at 2 ppm from December 31, 2022 and 1 ppm from December 31, 2023, and capped cosmetics at 10 ppm from December 31, 2022. The law let a manufacturer apply to the Department of Environmental Conservation for a waiver instead of meeting the cap. DEC publishes every waiver in one spreadsheet listing the manufacturer name, the product name, and the amount of 1,4-dioxane the manufacturer itself reported.

On the sheet covering waivers effective December 31, 2023 through December 30, 2024, the year the cap was 1 ppm, L'Oreal USA holds 69 product lines. They include Redken All Soft Shampoo at 4.50 ppm, Redken Color Extend Graydiant Shampoo at 3.67 ppm, Kerastase Densifique Women Bain at 4.60 ppm, and L'Oreal Professionnel Serie Expert Volumetry Shampoo at 7.23 ppm, which is more than seven times the legal cap. Twenty-one of the 69 were reported at 4 ppm or higher. On the previous sheet, covering waivers through December 30, 2023, the company holds 86 more lines.

L'Oreal USA does not appear on the final sheet, which covers waivers effective December 31, 2024 through December 30, 2025 and lists only 14 products from five other companies. DEC states that no waiver is effective after December 30, 2025 and that all products must comply with the limits.

Sources: https://dec.ny.gov/environmental-protection/pollution-prevention/household-personal-cosmetic-dioxane-limits and the waiver file it links, https://www.dec.ny.gov/fs/projects/waivers/1-4DApprovedWaivers.xlsx

survivors.felt_need: Her hair changed. It went dry and flat and the gray came in wiry, so she stopped buying the drugstore bottle and started paying thirty-eight dollars at the salon because the stylist said the cheap stuff was the problem. She has been buying safety. That is what the price tag was for.
survivors.counter: 1,4-dioxane is an unintended byproduct of making a mild surfactant, not an added ingredient, so the waiver reflects a manufacturing problem as much as a choice. L'Oreal did lower the levels and did comply by the deadline. And the ppm numbers on that list are self-reported by the manufacturer. New York's 1 ppm is also the strictest limit in the country. Federal law sets no limit whatsoever, which is the real point.

survivors.title: Is A Keratin Treatment Safe? (2026)
survivors.villain: GIB, LLC, trading as Brazilian Blowout. The California Attorney General settled with them on January 30, 2012 for labelling the Acai Smoothing Solution and the Professional Smoothing Solution as formaldehyde free when both released formaldehyde gas as soon as heat hit them. They paid $600,000, half of it Proposition 65 civil penalties. The words on the bottle were the lie, not the fine print inside it.
survivors.receipt:
VILLAIN: GIB, LLC, trading as Brazilian Blowout.

RECEIPT (verified on the page, January 30, 2012): California Attorney General Kamala D. Harris announced a settlement with GIB, LLC, doing business as Brazilian Blowout, requiring honest advertising of two salon smoothing products. The company agreed to pay $600,000, split as $300,000 in Proposition 65 civil penalties and $300,000 reimbursing the Attorney General's fees and costs. The two products were the Brazilian Blowout Acai Smoothing Solution and the Brazilian Blowout Professional Smoothing Solution, both marketed as formaldehyde free and safe. Both contained methylene glycol, which releases formaldehyde gas when heat is applied during the treatment. Under the settlement the company had to stop calling the products formaldehyde free and safe, run corrective advertising, put caution stickers on the bottles warning stylists that formaldehyde gas is emitted, issue accurate safety data sheets carrying Proposition 65 cancer warnings, retest for volatile organic compound compliance, and report the formaldehyde to California's Safe Cosmetics Program. It was the first government enforcement action in the United States over formaldehyde exposure from these products, and the first ever enforcement action under California's Safe Cosmetics Act of 2005.

CORRECTED SUPPORTING BEAT: California later went further. AB 2762, signed September 30, 2020, added Health and Safety Code section 108980, which bans formaldehyde (CAS no. 50-00-0), methylene glycol (CAS no. 463-57-0) and paraformaldehyde (CAS no. 30525-89-4) from cosmetics manufactured, sold or held for sale in California starting January 1, 2025. There is still no federal ban. FDA first targeted October 2023 to propose one, then pushed it to April 2024, November 2024, March 2025, July 2025, and finally December 2025, and let that one pass too. (Say "missed the deadline repeatedly, six times over three years," never "twice.")

SOURCES TO LINK: California Attorney General press release, January 30, 2012 (https://oag.ca.gov/news/press-releases/attorney-general-kamala-d-harris-announces-settlement-requiring-honest); the stipulated judgment PDF (https://oag.ca.gov/sites/all/files/agweb/pdfs/prop65/brazilian-blowout.pdf); California Health and Safety Code 108980; CNN, January 5, 2026 on the missed FDA deadline; CBS Los Angeles or NBC Bay Area, January 30-31, 2012 for the news account. Do NOT cite EWG, it dominates the FDA-delay coverage and is a banned source.

FRAMING: allegation and settlement language throughout. The Attorney General alleged, the company agreed, the company did not admit. Never state as fact that the products harmed anyone.

survivors.title: Are Makeup Remover Wipes Safe? What Kenvue Found in a Neutrogena Lot (2026)
survivors.villain: Kenvue Brands LLC, the company spun out of Johnson and Johnson that now owns Neutrogena. Its own internal quality testing turned up the bacteria, which means the testing worked and the manufacturing did not.
survivors.receipt:
Kenvue Brands LLC, the company spun out of Johnson and Johnson that now owns Neutrogena, voluntarily recalled 1,312 cases of Neutrogena Makeup Remover Ultra-Soft Cleansing Towelettes, lot number 1835U6325A, on September 19, 2025, after its OWN internal quality testing detected the bacterium Pluralibacter gergoviae. Kenvue's root cause analysis attributed the contamination to procedural deficiencies during manufacturing. The FDA classified the recall as Class II on October 3, 2025 (Event ID 97602, Recall Number C-0001-2026), its second-highest risk level, meaning exposure may cause temporary or medically reversible health consequences. The product had been distributed to Texas, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida. Pluralibacter gergoviae is associated with eye infections, urinary tract infections, respiratory infections and sepsis, particularly in people who are immune compromised or of advanced age.

CITATION CHANGE, REQUIRED: do not link globalcosmeticsnews.com, it 403s and is a trade newsletter rather than an approved source. Link instead to U.S. News & World Report (https://www.usnews.com/news/health-news/articles/2025-10-27/neutrogena-makeup-wipes-recalled-due-to-possible-bacteria) and NBC News (https://www.nbcnews.com/select/shopping/neutrogena-makeup-wipes-recall-2025-rcna239204), with the FDA enforcement report database (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/ires/index.cfm) as the primary record. DO NOT STATE A PACKAGE COUNT: sources split between 25-count and 50-count, so the post must omit it entirely.

The villain is Kenvue's manufacturing failure, a company that caught its own contamination after the product had already shipped to four states.
